question_english: If transaction A holds a shared lock R and if transaction B also requests for a shared lock on R, it will-
options: (a) result in a deadlock situation / एक डेडलॉक स्थिति में परिणाम होगा
(b) immediately be granted / तुरंत प्रदान किया जाएगा

technical_proof: Lock compatibility matrix: Shared(S) is compatible with Shared(S). Multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the same item simultaneously since shared locks only permit reads, which do not conflict with each other.
explanation: A shared lock (S) is also called a read lock. Multiple transactions can hold a shared lock on the same data item at the same time because they are only reading the data, not modifying it. In contrast, if a transaction holds an exclusive lock (X), no other transaction can acquire any lock (S or X) on it.
trap_point: Students confuse Shared-Shared compatibility with Shared-Exclusive incompatibility; remember S-S is always compatible.
memory_trick: S+S = Same time OK (both just reading); S+X or X+X = Wait.
revision_fact: Lock compatibility: S-S = Compatible, S-X = Incompatible, X-X = Incompatible.

explanation: Consistency guarantees that any business rule or invariant (here, x + y must remain constant) holds true before and after the transaction. The transaction only moves money between accounts; it never creates or destroys money.

question_english: Suppose a database system crashes again while recovering from a previous crash. Assume checkpointing is not done by the database either during the transactions or during recovery. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: (a) The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again. / फिर से रिकवरी करते समय उसी पूर्ववत और फिर से करने की सूची का उपयोग किया जाएगा।
(b) The system cannot recover any further. / सिस्टम और रिकवरी नहीं कर सकता।
(c) All the transactions that are already undone and redone will not recovered again. / वे सभी ट्रांजेक्शन जो पहले ही पूर्ववत और फिर से किए जा चुके हैं, फिर से रिकवर नहीं होंगे।
(d) The database will become inconsistent. / डेटाबेस असंगत हो जाएगा।
correct_answer: (a) The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again. / फिर से रिकवरी करते समय उसी पूर्ववत और फिर से करने की सूची का उपयोग किया जाएगा।
technical_proof: Without checkpointing, the system uses logs from the start to determine the undo/redo lists. Since logs are unaffected by the second crash (system logs persist on stable storage) and no checkpoint exists, the same undo/redo list is reconstructed and recovery is restarted from scratch, making the recovery process idempotent.
explanation: Without checkpointing, recovery always scans the log from the beginning to determine the undo and redo lists. If the system crashes again mid-recovery, it simply restarts and recomputes the exact same undo/redo list using the unaffected system logs, ensuring the process is idempotent (repeating it causes no inconsistency).
trap_point: Students think repeated crashes cause cascading inconsistency. In reality, log-based recovery is designed to be idempotent regardless of how many times it's interrupted.
memory_trick: No checkpoint = full log re-scan every time = same undo/redo list, no matter how many crashes occur.
revision_fact: Recovery using logs (without checkpoints) is idempotent — repeating it doesn't cause additional damage.
answer: (a) The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again. / फिर से रिकवरी करते समय उसी पूर्ववत और फिर से करने की सूची का उपयोग किया जाएगा।

question_english: A locked database file can be-
options: (a) Accessed by only one user / केवल एक उपयोगकर्ता द्वारा एक्सेस किया गया
(b) Modified by users with the correct password / सही पासवर्ड वाले उपयोगकर्ताओं द्वारा संशोधित
(c) Used to hide sensitive information / संवेदनशील जानकारी छिपाने के लिए उपयोग किया जाता है
(d) Updated by more than one user / एक से अधिक उपयोगकर्ताओं द्वारा अपडेट किया गया
correct_answer: (a) Accessed by only one user / केवल एक उपयोगकर्ता द्वारा एक्सेस किया गया
technical_proof: When a database file is locked (default behavior implies exclusive lock for a 'locked' file), only one user/process can access and modify it at a time. This is the fundamental purpose of locking — to prevent concurrent access conflicts.
explanation: Locking a file restricts access so that only one user or transaction can modify it at a given time, preventing data corruption from concurrent writes. By default, when a question says a file is simply 'locked' without specifying shared/exclusive, it implies exclusive lock behavior, meaning single-user access.
trap_point: Note this is distinct from Q22 on page 6, which presents a similar question but with a different correct answer (A) due to a slightly different option set including 'Both b and c'.
memory_trick: Locked file = Limited to one (by default, exclusive lock semantics).
revision_fact: A locked file, by default, restricts access to only one user at a time (exclusive lock semantics).

question_english: Which of the following scenarios may lead to an irrecoverable error in a database system?
options: (a) A transaction writes a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम लिखता है जब उसे एक अनकमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा पढ़ा जाता है
(b) A transaction reads a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम पढ़ता है जब उसे एक अनकमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा पढ़ा जाता है
(c) A transaction reads a data item after it is written by a committed transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम पढ़ता है जब उसे एक कमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा लिखा जाता है
(d) A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम पढ़ता है जब उसे एक अनकमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा लिखा जाता है
correct_answer: (d) A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम पढ़ता है जब उसे एक अनकमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा लिखा जाता है
technical_proof: Option (D) describes the classic 'Dirty Read' scenario (WR conflict where the reader sees uncommitted data). If the writing transaction later aborts, the reading transaction has already used invalid data, making the situation irrecoverable if the reader has already committed or taken external action.
explanation: This situation is called a 'Dirty Read'. If transaction T1 writes (updates) a value but hasn't committed yet, and T2 reads that uncommitted value, then if T1 later aborts, T2 has read data that never truly existed in a valid state. This can make the database inconsistent and irrecoverable, especially if T2 has already committed based on that dirty data.
trap_point: Options (A), (B), and (C) describe read-after-write-by-committed or read-after-read scenarios which are generally safe; only read-after-write-by-uncommitted (D) creates the classic dirty read problem.
memory_trick: Dirty Read = Reading 'dirty' (uncommitted) data that might vanish (rollback) later.
revision_fact: Dirty Read occurs when T2 reads data written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, T2's read becomes invalid/irrecoverable.
answer: (d) A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction / एक ट्रांजेक्शन एक डेटा आइटम पढ़ता है जब उसे एक अनकमिटेड ट्रांजेक्शन द्वारा लिखा जाता है

question_english: If several concurrent transactions are executed over the same data set and the second transaction updates the database before the first transaction is finished, the _______ property is violated and the database is no longer consistent.
technical_proof: Isolation specifically governs the independent execution of concurrent transactions, ensuring one transaction's intermediate state doesn't affect another. A second transaction interfering with the first before it finishes directly violates Isolation.
explanation: Isolation ensures that the execution of one transaction is not interfered with by other concurrently executing transactions. memory_trick: OLTP = Operational/Customer-facing transactions (banking, booking, retail); OLAP family = Analysis/Reporting.
revision_fact: OLTP is the customer-oriented system used by clerks, clients, and IT professionals for real-time transaction and query processing.

question_english: Which one of the following state transition is made when the transaction has been rolled back and the database is restored to the state prior to the start of the transition?
options: (a) Active → Partially Committed / एक्टिव → पार्शियली कमिटेड
(d) Partially Committed → Committed / पार्शियली कमिटेड → कमिटेड
technical_proof: In the standard transaction state diagram, when a failure occurs and a transaction is rolled back, restoring the database to its pre-transaction state, the transition is Active → Aborted (or Partially Committed → Aborted, depending on when the failure occurs). Since the question describes a rollback restoring to the state PRIOR to the transaction starting, Active → Aborted correctly captures this.
explanation: The standard transaction state diagram includes: Active → Partially Committed → Committed (success path), or Active/Partially Committed → Failed → Aborted (failure/rollback path). When a transaction is rolled back and the database is restored to its state before the transaction started, the transition is Active → Aborted.
trap_point: Students may confuse Active → Committed (success path, no rollback involved) with the rollback scenario, but Committed transactions cannot be rolled back via the standard transaction state model — only Active/Failed transactions move to Aborted.
memory_trick: Rollback = Abort. The 'Aborted' state means: as if the transaction never happened — DB restored to its pre-transaction state.
revision_fact: Active → Aborted is the transition when a transaction is rolled back, restoring the database to its pre-transaction state.

question_hindi: कई SQL ट्रांजैक्शंस के निष्पादन द्वारा उत्पन्न एक शेड्यूल पर विचार करें, जिनमें से प्रत्येक में READ ONLY एक्सेस-मोड है। निम्नलिखित में से किसकी गारंटी है?
question_english: Consider a schedule generated by the execution of several SQL transactions, each of which has READ ONLY access-mode. Which of the following is guaranteed?
options: (d) All the given options / दिए गए सभी विकल्प
correct_answer: (d) All the given options / दिए गए सभी विकल्प
technical_proof: Since all transactions are READ ONLY, no transaction modifies (writes) any data item. With no write operations, there can be no read-write or write-write conflicts at all — meaning every possible schedule is trivially conflict-serializable, serializable, and recoverable (since there is nothing to undo and no dirty data possible).
explanation: When every transaction has READ ONLY access mode, no transaction ever writes/modifies data. Without any writes, there are no conflicts (no RW or WW conflicts possible — only RR which never conflicts), so the schedule is automatically conflict-serializable. Since conflict-serializable implies serializable, and with no writes there's nothing to recover/undo, the schedule is also trivially recoverable. Hence all three properties are guaranteed.
trap_point: Students might think only one property (e.g., serializable) is guaranteed, missing that the complete absence of writes makes ALL listed properties trivially true simultaneously.
memory_trick: READ ONLY = No writes = No conflicts = Automatically serializable, conflict-serializable, AND recoverable, all at once.
revision_fact: A schedule with only READ ONLY transactions is automatically conflict-serializable, serializable, AND recoverable.
answer: (d) All the given options / दिए गए सभी विकल्प

explanation: COMMIT permanently saves all changes made during a transaction. ROLLBACK does the opposite — it undoes changes by reverting to the prior state. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deletes all rows from a table, unrelated to transaction persistence.

question_english: Which of the following is correct according to the technology deployed by DBMS?
options: (a) Pointers are used to maintain transactional integrity and consistency / पॉइंटर्स का उपयोग लेनदेन संबंधी अखंडता और स्थिरता बनाए रखने के लिए किया जाता है
(b) Cursors are used to maintain transactional integrity and consistency / कर्सर का उपयोग लेनदेन संबंधी अखंडता और स्थिरता बनाए रखने के लिए किया जाता है
(c) Locks are used to maintain transactional integrity and consistency / लॉक्स का उपयोग लेनदेन संबंधी अखंडता और स्थिरता बनाए रखने के लिए किया जाता है
(d) More than one of the above / उपयुक्त में से एक से अधिक
None of the above / उपयुक्त में से कोई नहीं
technical_proof: Locks are the standard DBMS concurrency control mechanism used to maintain transactional integrity and consistency by controlling concurrent access to data items, preventing conflicting simultaneous operations. Pointers (memory references) and Cursors (row-iteration mechanisms) serve entirely different purposes unrelated to transactional integrity enforcement.
explanation: Locking Protocol: when multiple users access data simultaneously, DBMS uses locks to control access. If a user is writing/modifying data, the DBMS locks that data so other users cannot modify it until the first operation completes, keeping data consistent. Pointers are memory address references, and cursors are used to iterate over query result sets row-by-row — neither relates to transactional integrity enforcement.
trap_point: Pointers and Cursors are real DBMS/programming concepts but serve completely different purposes (memory referencing and result-set iteration respectively) — they are not concurrency/integrity control mechanisms like Locks.
memory_trick: Locks = Lock the door to keep data Consistent and Integral; Pointers/Cursors are unrelated navigation/reference tools.
revision_fact: Locks are the technology DBMS uses to maintain transactional integrity and consistency during concurrent access.
